deep.reconstruction:
Setting (Gauss's own): alpha, beta, gamma are 'cyclic quantities', i.e. complex numbers of modulus 1. Each also names a point on the unit circle. Below I write alpha=e^{ia}, beta=e^{ib}, gamma=e^{ic}. The title 'Complexe Zahlen auf den Raum angewandt' means complex numbers applied to (plane) space. The previous page is dated 1852 Jul 29.

(1) Area of the inscribed triangle alpha, beta, gamma.
Gauss writes Delta = i(beta-alpha)(gamma-beta)(alpha-gamma)/(4 alpha beta gamma).
Expanding the numerator gives alpha^2 beta + beta^2 gamma + gamma^2 alpha - alpha beta^2 - beta gamma^2 - gamma alpha^2.
Dividing by alpha beta gamma gives Delta = (i/4)(beta/alpha + gamma/beta + alpha/gamma - alpha/beta - beta/gamma - gamma/alpha).
For the equilateral triangle the value is sqrt(27)/4.
Justification (mine): beta-alpha = e^{i(a+b)/2} * 2i sin((b-a)/2). Hence the product of the three differences is alpha beta gamma (2i)^3 s1 s2 s3, with s1, s2, s3 the half-difference sines. So Delta = 2 s1 s2 s3, which is the signed form of 2 sinA sinB sinC = abc/(4R) with R=1. Equivalently, Delta = -(1/2)[sin(b-a) + sin(c-b) + sin(a-c)], the shoelace formula.

(2) The tangential triangle, whose sides touch the unit circle at alpha, beta, gamma.
Its vertices are 2 beta gamma/(beta+gamma), 2 gamma alpha/(gamma+alpha) and 2 alpha beta/(alpha+beta). These are the intersections of pairs of tangents; the known identity is that the tangents at u and v meet at 2uv/(u+v).
Gauss gives its area as Delta' = i(gamma-beta)(alpha-gamma)(beta-alpha)/((gamma+beta)(alpha+gamma)(beta+alpha)), with equilateral value sqrt(27).
Justification (mine): (gamma-beta)/(gamma+beta) = i tan((c-b)/2). So Delta' = i * i^3 * t1 t2 t3 = tanA tanB tanC = tanA + tanB + tanC. This is the area of the tangential triangle of a triangle with circumradius 1, i.e. inradius 1 times the semiperimeter.

Centre of the circle circumscribed about the tangential triangle:
O' = 2 alpha beta gamma (alpha+beta+gamma)/((beta+gamma)(gamma+alpha)(alpha+beta)).
Verification (mine): put P = (alpha+beta)(beta+gamma)(gamma+alpha). Then 2 beta gamma/(beta+gamma) - O' = 2 beta gamma[(alpha+beta)(alpha+gamma) - alpha(alpha+beta+gamma)]/P = 2 beta^2 gamma^2/P. Cyclically, the other radius vectors are 2 gamma^2 alpha^2/P and 2 alpha^2 beta^2/P. All three have modulus 2/|P|, which is Gauss's statement: radius times |P| = 2.
The radius vectors equal (2 alpha beta gamma/P) * (beta gamma/alpha, gamma alpha/beta, alpha beta/gamma). Moreover P = alpha beta gamma * 8 cos((a-b)/2) cos((b-c)/2) cos((c-a)/2), so 2 alpha beta gamma/P is real. Hence the directions ('Klisen', inclinations) of beta gamma/alpha, alpha gamma/beta, alpha beta/gamma are, up to sign, those of the three radii. This is Gauss's last line.
Corollaries (mine, not stated by Gauss): O' is a real multiple of alpha+beta+gamma, the orthocentre, so it lies on the Euler line (this is the point X(26)). Also R' = 1/(4|cosA cosB cosC|); in the equilateral case R' = 2.
errors: The areas are signed. Formula (1) gives a negative value for a counterclockwise ordering of alpha, beta, gamma, and Gauss does not comment on this orientation convention.
For an obtuse inscribed triangle the tangent circle is an excircle of the tangential triangle. Formula (2) then still holds as a signed area (tanA tanB tanC < 0), but Gauss does not remark on it.
The final claim about 'Klisen' (directions) holds only up to a common real factor whose sign may be negative. That is, the directions agree up to reversal.

results.what: Area of a triangle inscribed in the unit circle: i(b-a)(c-b)(a-c)/(4abc), and the symmetric form (i/4)(sum of b/a - a/b)
results.modern_name: Complex-coordinate (unit-circle) area formula; equivalent to Area = abc/(4R) = 2R^2 sinA sinB sinC
results.usually_credited_to: Folklore of complex-number geometry (late 19th/20th c. treatments, e.g. Morley, Deaux, olympiad 'complex bashing')

results.what: Intersection of the tangents to the unit circle at u and v is 2uv/(u+v)
results.modern_name: Tangent-intersection formula in unit-circle complex coordinates

results.what: Area of the tangential triangle = i * prod(gamma-beta)/prod(gamma+beta) = tanA tanB tanC (R=1)
Circumcentre of the tangential triangle = 2abc(a+b+c)/((a+b)(b+c)(c+a)), circumradius = 2/|(a+b)(b+c)(c+a)|, radii directed along bc/a, ca/b, ab/c
results.modern_name: Circumcentre of the tangential triangle (Kimberling X(26)) on the Euler line; R' = R/(4|cosA cosB cosC|)
results.usually_credited_to: Classical triangle geometry (19th c.); complex form modern folklore

deep.surprise_reason: These are correct but elementary results of complex-coordinate triangle geometry. Gauss's use of complex numbers for plane geometry is well known. Still, a systematic unit-circle 'complex bash' (symmetric area formulas, the tangential triangle and its circumcentre X(26) in closed form) dated c. 1852 is a nice early instance of a method usually associated with later authors (Morley, Deaux). It is a notable unpublished detail but not a new theorem.

checkable.asserts: Radius vector from the circumcentre to vertex 2bc/(b+c) is 2b^2c^2/P (expected 0); by symmetry the other vertices give 2c^2a^2/P and 2a^2b^2/P, so the radius is 2/|P| on the unit circle
2uv/(u+v) lies on the tangent at u, since (p-u) is perpendicular to u (expected 0)

checkable.asserts: 2abc/P is real, so the radii point along bc/a, ca/b, ab/c and the centre is a real multiple of a+b+c (expected 0)

transcription_corrections: 'klisen' should be read 'Klisen' (capitalised noun). It is probably from Greek klisis, 'inclination', and means directions/arguments: 'the Klisen of beta gamma/alpha, alpha gamma/beta, alpha beta/gamma correspond to the three radii of this circle'.
The '= 2' is written in the manuscript above the 'Klisen' line but belongs to the preceding sentence: 'Product des Halbmessers in den Modulus von (beta+gamma)(gamma+alpha)(alpha+beta) = 2'.
'des darum beschriebenen Kreises' is correct; 'des' is overwritten (dem->des) and 'Kreises' is corrected over another word.
The struck-through 'Cd 1' and '1576/3' at top right, the circled '15' and the bottom-right 'G.-Nummer 5.' are archival/library annotations, not Gauss's text.
